contributions.headingText: SDH-deficient tumour syndromes is a group of syndromes characterized by neoplasias deficient in succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), usually associated with germline (constitutional) pathogenic sequence variants in one of the SDH genes encoding the subunits of SDH (SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2) or with epimutation (promoter hypermethylation) of the SDHC gene.

168000 Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 1; PPGL1 (SDHD)

601650 Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 2; PPGL2 (SDHAF2)

605373 Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 3; PPGL3 (SDHC)

115310 Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 4; PPGL4 (SDHB)

614165 Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma syndrome 5; PPGL5 (SDHA)

604287 Carney triad

Acceptable: hereditary phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndromes 1 to 5 (phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndrome 1, phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndrome 2, phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndrome 3, phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndrome 4, phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndrome 5); Carney triad (restricted to syndromic but non-hereditary disease).

Not recommended: Carney–Stratakis dyad/syndrome.

Phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndrome 1 (germline SDHD pathogenic variants); phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndrome 2 (germline SDHAF2 pathogenic variants); phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndrome 3 (germline SDHC pathogenic variants); phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndrome 4 (germline SDHB pathogenic variants); phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma syndrome 5 (germline SDHA pathogenic variants); Carney triad (restricted to syndromic but non-hereditary disease, where no germline SDH pathogenic variant has been identified)

Phaeochromocytomas/paragangliomas are the most common manifestations followed by SDH-deficient gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) and SDH-deficient renal cell carcinomas. Pituitary neuroendocrine tumours (PitNETs) / pituitary adenomas and pulmonary chondromas are recognized associations but are much less common. There are strong but inconsistent genotype–phenotype correlations so that different genes are more commonly associated with certain tumour combinations and locations. However, there is overlap between all of the SDH-deficient tumour syndromes. SDH pathogenic variants are associated more commonly with extra-adrenal paragangliomas and less commonly with adrenal phaeochromocytomas. The extra-adrenal tumours can be located in the head and neck, thorax, or abdomen and are associated with SDHB, SDHC, or SDHD pathogenic variants as outlined in #37220Table 3.02. SDHB pathogenic variants are most frequently identified in patients with intra-abdominal extra-adrenal paragangliomas and/or with metastatic paraganglioma, while pathogenic variants in the SDHD gene are more common in patients with head-and-neck paragangliomas {29239034}. SDH-deficient GISTs are most strongly associated with SDHC epimutation or SDHA pathogenic variants {29239034}. With the exception of a single case report, all well-characterized SDH-deficient GISTs reported to date have arisen in the stomach {20305538;21997692;28324028}. As their names indicate, renal cell carcinomas arise in the kidneys, PitNETs / pituitary adenomas in the sella turcica (with the exception of ectopic manifestations), and pulmonary chondromas in the lungs. SDH-deficient renal cell carcinomas usually harbour SDHB or SDHC pathogenic variants (less commonly SDHA and very rarely, if at all, SDHD) {33664427}. Pulmonary chondromas are commonly associated with SDHC epimutation (Carney triad) but are very rare in other SDH-deficient syndromes.

Because of the close embryological origin to paragangliomas and phaeochromocytomas, neuroblastomas have also been investigated for the occurrence of SDHA and SDHB variants. However, although cases of neuroblastoma have been reported in the presence of pathogenic SDH variants {20503330;30068732}, the relationship is sufficiently rare that causality is uncertain.

Clinical features vary according to both genotype and tumour location {22544211;29239034;24625421;20305538;31789631;32251007}. SDHB-related phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma typically exhibits a noradrenergic biochemical profile (even when confined to the adrenal medulla), reflected by increases in plasma and/or urine noradrenaline or particularly its metabolite, normetanephrine. These tumours may also be characterized by the production of dopamine and its metabolite, 3-methoxytyramine, which are often secreted together with normetanephrine. In general, abdominal paragangliomas are more commonly associated with production of noradrenaline. Although rarely they may be biochemically silent and clinically asymptomatic {18840642;31194241}, those that are secretory may give rise to classic clinical symptoms and signs related to catecholamine excess, such as hypertensive crises. In contrast, head-and-neck paragangliomas usually present as mass lesions that are clinically silent, although they frequently produce dopamine and, in a very small minority of cases, noradrenaline, which may be detected by elevated levels of 3-methoxytyramine or normetanephrine. Although tumours other than SDH-deficient phaeochromocytoma–paraganglioma, GIST, renal carcinoma, pulmonary chondroma, and PitNET / pituitary adenoma have been reported in SDH pathogenic variant carriers, it is likely that these are incidental findings in closely monitored populations {29239034}. A family history of disease is commonly absent, and SDHD and SDHAF2 show parent-of-origin effects on penetrance so that symptomatic disease is almost always only inherited from a paternal carrier {21862453;21937622;25300370;27856506}. Twenty-four-hour urinary or plasma normetanephrine, metanephrine, and 3-methoxytyramine levels (in plasma) may be used to identify early disease in asymptomatic carriers.

At least 40% of paragangliomas and phaeochromocytomas in adults are hereditary {29239044} and close to half of all genetically determined cases are associated with one of the SDH deficiency syndromes – more if paraganglioma or phaeochromocytoma is diagnosed during childhood {22544211;29239034;21969497;32432211;33682326}. SDH-deficient GISTs account for 3% of all GISTs in an unselected adult population, but account for the great majority of GISTs diagnosed in children {20305538;21997692}. SDH-deficient renal cell carcinomas account for < 0.05–0.2% of all renal carcinomas {25025441}, but are overrepresented in young adults (median age: 35 years, range: 14–76 years) {25025441;25034258}. SDH-deficient PitNETs / pituitary adenomas are rare (< 0.3% of unselected tumours) {24625421}. Pulmonary chondromas are typically found in young women and are very rare outside the setting of Carney triad {18043038;31236950;19723753}.

Contrasting with many other hereditary syndromes, biallelic somatic inactivation of the SDH genes in tumours is very unusual in the absence of germline pathogenic variants (or, less commonly, postzygotic epimutation or mosaicism) of one of the SDH genes {29239034}.

The term “Carney triad” is now restricted to syndromic, but non-hereditary, disease where no germline SDH pathogenic variant has been identified by clinically deployed testing methodologies. Carney triad is most commonly associated with postzygotic SDHC promoter hypermethylation (epimutation), but may also be explained by other pathogenic genetic events not detected by some testing methodologies – for example, constitutional mosaicism not detected in DNA extracted from blood samples subjected to Sanger sequencing but potentially identifiable by massively parallel sequencing with many reads, or by deep-intronic genetic variants not identified in some panels. It should be noted that Carney triad is unrelated to Carney complex, which is a different inherited neoplasia syndrome caused by germline variants in PRKAR1A {27875378;33444222} (see section Carney complex (PRKAR1A, PDE8B, PDE11A)).

Mitochondrial complex 2, also known as the SDH complex, is a key mitochondrial enzyme which links the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain {22544211;29239034}. It is encoded by four nuclear autosomal genes but assembled at the inner mitochondrial membrane. It is composed of four protein subunits: SDHC and SDHD (the anchoring components) and SDHA and SDHB (the catalytic components). Additionally, SDHAF2 is required for flavination of the SDHA protein. If any component of the SDH complex is lost or dysfunctional, the entire SDH complex becomes unstable, and the SDHB subunit is released into the cytoplasm, where it rapidly degrades, accounting for the loss of expression of SDHB protein {19576851;22544211;22835832;29239034}. Dysfunction of this key enzyme causes the accumulation of succinate, which acts as an oncometabolite behaving as a competitor of 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases involved in a broad spectrum of tumorigenic pathways, including hypoxic regulation and epigenetic reprogramming {15987702;32234487}.

Although multifocality is an important clue, the phaeochromocytomas, paragangliomas, PitNETs / pituitary adenomas, and renal cell carcinomas associated with SDH pathogenic variants grossly resemble their sporadic counterparts. SDH-deficient GISTs are commonly multilobulated or plexiform, and more frequently show lymph node metastases {20305538;21997692;21753704}.

Loss of expression of SDHB (termed SDH deficiency) occurs whenever there is biallelic inactivation of any component of the SDH complex (that is, SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, or SDHAF2) {22544211;29239034;24625421;20305538;31789631;32251007}. Somatic-only pathogenic variants of both alleles of SDH family genes do occur but are extremely rare {17634472}, and therefore SDH deficiency is prima facie evidence of an SDH-deficient tumour syndrome. Tumours with biallelic inactivation of SDHA show SDHA loss in addition to SDHB loss, whereas tumours associated with SDHB, SDHC, or SDHD pathogenic variants, or SDHC epimutation, demonstrate preserved expression of SDHA {21752896;23060355}. SDHB and SDHA immunohistochemistry may be difficult to interpret in some cases, and a tumour should only be considered deficient if there is preserved expression in non-neoplastic cells, which act as internal controls. SDHB immunohistochemistry can be particularly valuable in assessing whether a particular tumour found in a patient with a germline SDH family pathogenic variant is actually caused by tumoural loss of SDH {30273935}, and whether a variant of unknown significance identified by genetic testing is pathogenic. Normal SDHA and SDHB immunostaining is granular and cytoplasmic (mitochondrial). In some SDH-deficient tumours, particularly SDHD-related tumours, interpretation may be particularly challenging because a cytoplasmic blush is often retained. In this setting, weak diffuse expression in neoplastic cells, which contrasts with the strong distinctly granular expression in internal positive controls, is a useful clue to the diagnosis of SDH deficiency {19576851;29239034}. Some phaeochromocytomas not associated with SDH family pathogenic variants but arising in the setting of von Hippel–Lindau syndrome (or with somatic biallelic VHL inactivation) may show very weak expression of SDHB, which can be mistaken for SDH deficiency {29239034}. Other markers of SDH deficiency may be useful when SDHB is difficult to interpret. For example, α-inhibin and CAIX are more commonly expressed in SDH- and VHL-related (so-called pseudohypoxic pathway–related cluster 1 disease) phaeochromocytomas and paragangliomas, respectively, than in other tumours, but these markers lack sensitivity and specificity {23257898;31383958;33826547}.

Some SDH-deficient paragangliomas, especially those in the head and neck, are characterized by well-formed, almost circular, nests of epithelioid cells, sometimes with focally clear or vacuolated cytoplasm {31789631}. However, this morphology is inconsistent and does not replace SDHB immunohistochemistry, which is recommended in all phaeochromocytomas and paragangliomas.

There are several morphological, clinical, and molecular clues to the identification of SDH-deficient GISTs. These include gastric location, multifocality, a plexiform or multinodular growth pattern, epithelioid cell type predominance sometimes with a vaguely nested architecture, and relatively frequent lymph node metastasis (summarized in #37221Table 3.03) {20305538;21753704;29239034}. Although SDH-deficient GISTs are not associated with KIT or PDGFRA pathogenic variants, they virtually always show diffuse strong immunohistochemical expression of both KIT and DOG1 {20305538;21753704;29239034}. This can be useful in the differential diagnosis with PDGFRA-mutant GISTs, which may resemble SDH-deficient GISTs owing to their frequent gastric location and epithelioid cell predominance, but commonly show patchy or absent KIT expression. These morphological and immunohistochemical features can be subtle and a low threshold for performing SDHB and SDHA immunohistochemistry is recommended for any gastric GIST {20305538;21997692;21753704}. As with other SDH-deficient tumours, there is almost always only one driver gene variant in SDH-deficient GISTs. However, a single reported tumour with a germline SDHB and somatic KRAS pathogenic variant exhibited unusual morphology, including very small epithelioid cells, a very high proliferative fraction, and only patchy KIT and DOG1 expression. The tumour progressed rapidly, with a fatal outcome {27011036;29967109}.

SDH-deficient renal cell carcinomas are now recognized as a distinct entity {21934479;25034258;25025441;33664427;29386252;34949766}. They usually show distinctive morphological features at least focally, being comprised of sheets or compact nests of bland cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm. The eosinophilic cytoplasm lacks the fine homogeneous granularity of oncocytoma and may have a flocculent quality. Microcystic change is common {21934479;25025441;25034258;34949766}. A characteristic but inconstant feature of SDH-deficient renal carcinoma is the presence of cytoplasmic inclusions containing eosinophilic or bubbly pale material {21934479;25034258;25025441;33664427;34949766}. Higher-grade transformation may occur in SDH-deficient renal carcinomas and is heralded by denser cytoplasm, increased nuclear atypia with prominent nucleoli, coagulative necrosis, and occasionally sarcomatoid changes. Other morphologies are described and appear to be associated with worse prognosis {34949766}. Non-SDH–related kidney tumours with very clear cytoplasm, such as clear cell renal carcinomas, may show markedly decreased expression of SDHB, a reflection of their cleared cytoplasm with few mitochondria, which should not be mistaken for SDH deficiency {29180251;33526874;33664427}. In these cases, morphological correlation is key.

Experience with SDH-deficient PitNETs / pituitary adenomas is limited. According to some reports they may be larger at diagnosis and more frequently prolactin producing {25695889;24625421;24096523;23633203;29239034}. However, suggestions of other morphological clues have not been confirmed {25695889;24625421;24096523;23633203;29239034}.

SDH-deficient pulmonary chondromas lack atypia and frequently show calcification. In contrast to pulmonary hamartomas, they usually demonstrate a smooth contour, do not show entrapped respiratory epithelium between the lobules of cartilage, and do not contain other mesenchymal elements, such as fat, smooth muscle, or myxoid spindle cells. Although SDHB immunohistochemistry may assist in the diagnosis of syndromic chondromas, it is less reliable in this setting {31236950;29239034}.

The diagnosis of SDH-deficient tumours can occasionally be suggested on cytology if the morphology is compatible and there is material for immunohistochemistry. However, as firm diagnosis requires loss of SDHB expression in the presence of an internal positive control, extreme care is warranted when interpreting SDHB immunohistochemistry on small biopsies and cell block preparations, which may be subject to both false positive and false negative interpretations.

Because pathogenic biallelic somatic-only variants are rare, the diagnosis of any SDH-deficient neoplasm is considered an indication for genetic counselling/testing {32412940}. Close collaboration between geneticists and pathologists is important because various analyses based on tumoural tissues can strongly contribute to genetic diagnosis {30877234;28070496;27857127}. Immunohistochemistry for SDHB and SDHA can be very useful to assess the pathogenicity of genetic variants of uncertain significance in the SDH genes {25720320}. Germline pathogenic variants in SDHA appear to be relatively common (estimated to occur in as many as 0.3% of the Dutch population) {21752896} but demonstrate a low lifetime penetrance (estimated as 1.7%, but in practice the clinical penetrance may be lower) {30201732}. Therefore, the clinical significance of SDHA variants, particularly if identified by large panel sequencing in the absence of SDH-deficient neoplasia, should be carefully considered and interpreted in the clinical context {21752896;23060355}. Given the low penetrance, recommendations vary for surveillance and cascade testing of family members in the setting of SDHA variants {29978154;34021277}.

The term “Carney triad” is appropriate when no germline SDH variant is identified in an individual with syndromic, but not hereditary, disease. Given that somatic biallelic variants in the SDH genes are rare, it is reasonable to assign a presumptive diagnosis of Carney triad to any patient with an SDH-deficient neoplasm and no proven germline SDH variant, unless biallelic somatic-only variants have been demonstrated. Current evidence suggests that Carney triad is usually associated with postzygotic mosaic epimutation (promoter hypermethylation) of SDHC {24859990;25540324;33624983}, which can only be identified by specific DNA methylation assays that are not widely available. However, it should be noted that mosaicism for germline SDH pathogenic variants also occurs and might not be detected by sequencing when the variant allelic ratio is low {31046099}. Some patients previously given the clinical diagnosis of Carney triad, on the basis of syndromic SDH-deficient neoplasia in the absence of an identifiable pathogenic variant, may carry deep-intronic pathogenic sequence variants that were previously unrecognized {33195952}.

Essential: confirmed pathogenic or likely pathogenic sequence variant in one of SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, or SDHAF2, or SDHC epimutation; OR the presence of more than one confirmed SDH-deficient neoplasm in an individual or family.

Desirable: identification of even a single SDH-deficient neoplasm is presumptive evidence of syndromic disease unless pathogenic somatic-only biallelic variants can be proven; therefore, exclusion of rare pathogenic somatic-only biallelic variants may have a role if no germline sequence variants are identified.

Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) / American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM staging is applicable to individual malignant tumours.

In view of the strongly syndromic nature of SDH-deficient neoplasia, surveillance and follow-up for other SDH-deficient neoplasms is indicated even in cases where no germline pathogenic sequence variant has been identified {34021277}. Paragangliomas associated with SDHB pathogenic variants appear to have a higher risk of metastasis {29239034;34021277}. The clinical behaviour of SDH-deficient GISTs is not predictable by the risk stratification parameters of size and mitotic count applied to other GISTs {20305538;21753704}. SDH-deficient renal cell carcinomas with conventional morphology are low-risk malignancies; however, the presence of high-grade nuclear atypia, tumour necrosis, or variant morphologies predicts a high risk of aggressive behaviour {25025441;34949766}.
